opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinctive thing a company like Anthropic brings is credibility on a particular kind of claim. When a nonprofit says "this technology could be dangerous and we need guardrails," a lot of policymakers hear that as coming from people who are maybe a bit removed from the action, or who have an ideological axe to grind. When a company at the frontier says "we're building this, we see what it can do, and we think regulation is warranted, even regulation that constrains us," that lands differently. It's a costly signal. You're arguing against your own short-term commercial interest, and people notice that.

There's also the practical knowledge piece. A frontier developer can speak concretely about what a safety framework looks like in practice, what testing for dangerous capabilities actually involves, what's feasible to ask companies to do and what's just going to be compliance theater. That kind of detail is really valuable when you're trying to write rules that work rather than rules that sound good. Nonprofits can develop a lot of that expertise, but there's no substitute for having actually tried to implement these things inside an organization shipping products.

And I think there's an existence-proof role. If one company adopts something like a responsible scaling policy and keeps competing, it becomes much harder for others to say "that's impossible" or "that would kill innovation." That makes it easier for policymakers to require it.

That said, I don't think companies should be the main voice, and I'd be wary of anyone who thinks they should be. Companies have conflicts of interest, even well-intentioned ones, and there will always be a pull toward the version of regulation that happens to suit you. Nonprofits can say things companies can't. They can be more ambitious, more critical, push on what's needed rather than what's palatable to an industry. So I see it as complementary: the company provides credibility, technical grounding and proof of feasibility, and independent organizations provide the pressure and the scrutiny, including scrutiny of the companies themselves. You probably want both, and you want them to sometimes disagree.

r001.rationale: The response says nonprofits can be more ambitious and provide independent scrutiny, but it does not identify perceived neutrality relative to companies as their advantage. It even notes that policymakers may see nonprofits as having an ideological axe to grind.

r002.rationale: The response says a company’s example can counter claims that regulation would kill innovation, but it does not identify politicians’ interest in effects on business or the economy as a source of companies’ advocacy advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is just credibility and concreteness. When a nonprofit goes to a policymaker and says, "AI could be really dangerous, here's what we think you should do," that's useful, but it's a little abstract. When a company that's actually building frontier models shows up and says, "Here's what we're seeing in our own systems, here's what our safety testing looks like, here's where we think we and our competitors could be doing better, and here's a specific requirement we'd be willing to be held to," that lands differently. Policymakers are used to companies lobbying for less regulation. A company asking for well-designed rules on itself is a weird enough signal that people pay attention.

The second thing is detail. A lot of the hard part of AI policy isn't deciding that safety matters, it's figuring out what the actual mechanics should be. What does a reasonable evaluation regime look like? What counts as a dangerous capability threshold? How do you write a transparency requirement that's meaningful without being impossible to comply with? Those are questions where you need people who've actually run the evals, who know what's feasible on what timeline, who know where the loopholes would be. Companies have that knowledge in a way most outside groups just don't, and I think the responsible thing is to share it rather than hoard it.

I'd also say there's a demonstration effect. If a frontier lab publishes a responsible scaling policy, or commits to third-party testing, or publishes its model cards in a certain way, that creates an existence proof. It becomes harder for other companies to say "that's not practical," and it gives policymakers something concrete to point to when they're drafting requirements.

Now, I want to be honest about the limits here, because they're real. A company has commercial interests, and you should assume that colors things, even with the best intentions. There's an obvious risk of advocating for rules that happen to favor incumbents, or quietly softening positions when they'd be costly. So I don't think the right picture is "companies should lead on policy." I think it's more that companies and nonprofits are complementary. Nonprofits and academics can be the independent check, they can push for things that aren't in any company's interest, they can say "that proposal from the lab is weaker than it should be." And companies can bring the technical grounding and the willingness to actually be regulated. The ecosystem works best when both are there and neither fully trusts the other.

r001.rationale: The response describes nonprofits and academics as an independent check that can push for policies outside a company’s interests, identifying their relative independence as an advocacy advantage.

r002.rationale: The response cites companies’ technical knowledge and credibility with policymakers, but does not identify policymakers’ interest in effects on business or the economy as a source of companies’ advantage.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinctive contribution is being able to connect policy proposals to what’s actually happening inside a company building these systems. A nonprofit can do excellent work asking what rules would be desirable. But there are some questions where it really helps to have people who can say, “Here’s how we would implement that. Here’s what we can currently measure. Here’s where the proposed requirement would miss the thing you’re worried about.”

A company can also try things internally. If you think companies should evaluate their models for dangerous capabilities and take additional precautions when they see certain results, you can start doing that yourself. That gives you something concrete to point to in policy discussions, including evidence about what’s difficult and what needs to improve.

Of course, being a company also creates conflicts of interest. I wouldn’t want policymakers to treat a company’s view as an impartial assessment of what society needs. Independent nonprofits have a really important role in challenging those views. But technical detail, practical experience, and a willingness to demonstrate the practices you’re advocating—that’s a contribution an AI company is particularly well placed to make.

r001.rationale: The response notes companies’ conflicts of interest and says nonprofits can challenge their views, but it does not identify nonprofits’ perceived neutrality as an advantage in policy advocacy.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention politicians’ interest in how policies affect businesses or the economy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinctive contribution is being able to connect policy ideas to what’s actually happening inside a company building these systems. A nonprofit can make the case for a particular safeguard, and that can be really valuable. An AI company can say, “Here’s how we would implement it, here’s what we’ve tried, here’s what would be difficult, and here’s what we think other companies could reasonably be asked to do.” That can make a proposal much more concrete.

There’s also something valuable about a company saying, “We think this requirement should apply to us.” That doesn’t settle whether it’s a good requirement, but it can help move the conversation beyond the assumption that industry will oppose any regulation.

The obvious caveat is that companies have commercial interests. You shouldn’t treat their policy positions as disinterested judgments about the public good. I’d see this as complementary to nonprofits: companies can contribute technical knowledge and experience implementing safeguards, while independent organizations can scrutinize the proposals and ask whether they’re actually sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response notes companies’ commercial interests and nonprofits’ independent scrutiny, but it does not identify nonprofits’ perceived neutrality as an advocacy advantage.

r002.rationale: The response says companies can explain implementation and feasibility, but it does not mention politicians’ interest in business or economic effects as a source of companies’ advantage.
